extracted.intended_audience: geologists, natural philosophers, and educated readers interested in physical geography and volcanology (19th-century observational science)
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive, observational treatment of volcanic activity, mud volcanoes, thermal and cold springs, and related hydrothermal and gaseous emanations; emphasizes classification, origin hypotheses, and field examples. Intended as natural-history/geognostic exposition rather than experimental protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a true volcano
rubrics_metrics.description: "A volcano, properly so called, exists only where a permanent connection is established between the interior of the earth and the atmosphere, and the reaction of the interior on the surface then continues during long periods of time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a classificatory criterion: intermittent or short-lived connections (closed channels) do not constitute a true volcano; permanence of communication and long-term activity are required. Example/qualification: activity may be interrupted for centuries (e.g., Vesuvius 'Fisove').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between salses (mud volcanoes) and true volcanoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Salses (mud volcanoes) "disengage little else but carbureted hydrogen, together with bitumen and other products of the distillation of coal, and pour forth no other torrents except of mud..." whereas true volcanoes generate sulphureted hydrogen and muriatic acid, upheave tracts of land, and emit streams of melted feldspathic materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification hinges on emitted materials and eruptive behaviour: salses often show initial fiery explosions but typically produce cold mud flows, gas (hydrogen, carbonic acid, nitrogen) and bitumen rather than lava; they are a transitional phenomenon between springs/earthquakes and igneous volcanism. Field examples: Jokmali, Baklichli, Monte Ziblo, Macalubi (Sicily).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum/taxonomy of volcanic and related phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Must distinguish among earthquakes, thermal/aqueous/gaseous springs, mud volcanoes (salses), bell-formed or dome-shaped trachytic rocks without openings, craters of elevation, and permanent igneous volcanoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use morphological and dynamic criteria (presence/absence of openings, emitted products, continuity of connection with interior, occurrence of lava flows) to place phenomena along a continuum from weak/episodic to strongly igneous activity. This taxonomy guides interpretation of origin and expected behaviours (e.g., eruptions, emissions, elevation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of thermal springs and controls on spring temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: The temperature of springs depends on the temperature of the stratum of origin, the specific heat of the soil, and the quantity and temperature of meteoric water; deeper sources and contact with subterranean heat produce hotter springs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical indicators: deepest artesian wells are warmest (Arago); highest measured permanent spring temperatures (203–209°F) indicate deep origin (~7140 ft estimated for some springs). Springs near active volcanoes can be cooler (97–130°F) due to differing mechanisms. Mixing of waters (mountain/runoff) complicates interpretation of spring temperature as a direct measure of subterranean heat. Examples: Aguas Calientes de las Trincheras (206.6°F), Jorullo hot springs (186.4°F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using flowing springs to determine isogeothermal lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of 'isogeothermal' (chthonisothermal) lines from flowing springs is difficult because of blending of waters from different heights/depths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for mixing of mountain-origin waters with deep-rising waters; only springs unmixed and having long subsurface course (depths cited: 40–60 ft in temperate zones; ~1 foot in equinoctial regions per Boussingault) reliably indicate mean subsurface temperature. Use careful field assessment of source and flow-path to avoid misattribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth at which ground temperature becomes invariant (practical criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cold springs indicate mean atmospheric temperature only when unmixed and when they have passed through a long course at a depth equal to about 40–60 feet in temperate latitudes and, according to Boussingault, about one foot in equinoctial regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these depth thresholds when using subsurface temperature as climate proxy; beware of shallow mixing and surface influences (meteoric inputs). Table of tropical station examples illustrates correspondence between shallow-ground and air mean temperatures (Guayaquil, Anserma Nuevo, Zupia, Popayan, Quito).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity and temperature relation of the hottest permanent springs
rubrics_metrics.description: The hottest permanent springs (between 203° and 209°) are remarkably the purest, holding the smallest quantity of mineral substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe mineral content as well as temperature; very hot springs may show greater variability in temperature over decades compared with moderately hot springs (122°–165°), which have shown remarkable invariability in heat and mineral contents over long periods. Historical chemical analyses (Boussingault) show temporal changes (e.g., Las Trincheras rose 12° over 23 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of travertine from thermal waters
rubrics_metrics.description: Thermal water, impregnated with carbonic acid and sulphurous gases, continually forms horizontally-ranged strata of limestone (travertine) or conical elevations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travertine formation is predicted where thermal waters rich in CO2 and sulphurous vapors flow and precipitate carbonates; such deposits can preserve vegetation remains (example: Van Diemen's Land travertine with extinct vegetation per Darwin). Use geochemical context (gas content, temperature) to anticipate travertine deposition and morphology (horizontal strata vs conical mounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mud-volcano lifecycle and indicators of source depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Mud volcanoes often show an initial violent explosion of fire, followed by long-duration weak activity; subsequent cold mud emissions indicate that the ongoing seat of the phenomenon is near the surface and that communication with deep hot strata is soon closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations of source depth should consider post-eruption cooling and closure of deep channels. Large early flames indicate brief deep connections; persistent mud flows and cool emissions point to shallow ongoing activity. Historical eruption behaviours (Jokmali, Baklichli) and gas compositions (hydrogen with naphtha, carbonic acid, or near-pure nitrogen in some cases) inform classification and hazard assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcano morphology: craters of elevation versus eruptive cones
rubrics_metrics.description: Craters of elevation are produced by elastic vapors elevating portions of the crust into dome-shaped unopened masses (trachyte/dolerite); such craters often show no eruptive phenomena and may be later filled with water or colonized by corallines if uplifted from the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish elevation-formed craters from erupted cones by presence/absence of channels and ejected materials. The origin influences island physiognomy and landscape (examples: Palma, Nisyros) and constrains expectations about future eruptive activity (no permanent channel → no volcano).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between volcano height and eruption frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Eruptions are observed to be more frequent in low than in elevated volcanoes; if the volcanic focus lies at equal depth, raising fused masses to greater elevations requires more force, which correlates with longer intervals between eruptions. The permanence of the channel of communication also modulates frequency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elevation as one factor (alongside channel permanence) to assess eruption likelihood and recurrence intervals. Examples given: Stromboli (2318 ft) nearly continuously active vs Cotopaxi (19,069 ft) with long quiet intervals. Exceptions may result from varying permanence of subsurface channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcano origin model: elevation of soft masses vs accumulation of lava
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to the notion of gradual accumulation of ejected lava, mountains termed 'volcanoes' seem to originate more often from the sudden elevation of soft masses of trachyte or labradoritic augite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting volcanic origins and landform evolution, consider structural uplift and doming by elastic forces as primary origin mechanisms in many cases, rather than sole accumulation of erupted lava. Morphology (conical vs elongated forms), internal rock types, and presence/absence of surrounding ejecta help discriminate the origin mechanism (example: Pichincha rises immediately from plateau and is not always conical).
